A series production of 30-40 parts would be considered a big run, with a specific example being nuclear applications that often require a run of 20 pieces. Following prior facility models, the DOE prefers to purchase finished copper accelerators from industry. Currently there is no vendor with all of the required technology in-house required to manufacture a finished EBW copper accelerator. RadiaBeam Technologies has developed in-house capabilities and a network of partners for production of brazed copper accelerating structures utilizing a combination of internal capabilities and external vacuum brazing service providers. The current DOE model is that the private industry should bear the risk of the investment and amortize the cost of investing in facilities over 10 years. Both DOD and DOE primes have discussed this cost-share framework for equipment and facilities with job shops. The major concern is which party owns the risk and the lack of guarantee of funding over the period of amortization. In fact, contracts are seldom guaranteed for 1 year: and previous US accelerator companies went bankrupt when they invested in the required equipment for manufacturing accelerators and the contract was then awarded to a foreign entity. A similar issue was encountered with a job shop investing in manufacturing accelerators for a DOE National Lab. The job shop invested in the internal forming, machining, pre-weld etch and welding equipment and developed an external partnership for heavy etching, electropolishing and clean room assembly. The National Lab customer would not accept having dependency on external Lab so the contract was not completed at a loss for the job shop. Fortunately, the job shop properly budgeted and planned for this possibility and the loss of business was not fatal to the company. With the potential risk and the evidence of past bad faith relationships, it is unlikely private industry would make the significant investment for copper accelerator manufacturing via electron beam welding. Because of the high risk of ownership, the DOE could purchase and own the equipment for the private company with a agreed upon buy-back with the OEM if the venture did not work economically. While this distributes the risk between DOE and private company, it can become a complex accounting practice.
